articles.title: The race for 2028 is on as Republicans unpack midterm disaster
articles.summary: Top contenders eyeing the 2028 Republican primary to replace Donald Trump worked to unpack what went wrong in their party's disastrous midterm election.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Vice President JD Vance blamed the midterm shellacking on the war in Iran. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said an "economic disconnect" also led to sweeping Republican losses. And Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis boasted that his state was the only GOP stronghold to survive the blue tsunami.

After Democrats' midterm rout , the race for 2028 on the Republican side is on.

Top contenders eyeing the 2028 Republican primary to replace Donald Trump worked to unpack what went wrong for their party after a decisive repudiation of Trump in the Nov. 3 midterms. And in their respective critiques, Vance, Cruz and DeSantis started to look beyond the term-limited ‒ and now lame-duck ‒ president who has dominated their party for a decade.

"Let's be clear about what happened last night: This is as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years," DeSantis said .

In a historic rebuke of the party in power, Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and Senate, winning reliably red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, and flipping House seats across the country that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.

Vance, in a Nov. 4 postmortem analysis on X , said MAGA voters turned out to the polls in solid numbers, but he observed that "many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026." Above all, Vance blamed the war on Iran, which the president defended throughout the campaign, even as gas prices spiked as a result of the conflict.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance said, referring to Trump telling Fox News "a part of" the midterm collapse was because of Iran. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

"But everyone knows why we lost," said Vance, who has taken on a leading role in negotiations to end the war. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

In an appeal to Republicans upset with the midterm outcome, Vance said, "Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

Although they've not formally entered the 2028 Republican primary, Vance and Cruz are widely expected to run for the party's nomination, while DeSantis is considered a potential candidate as well. Any announcements on candidacies may not take place until 2027. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also considered a possible 2028 contender , has yet to publicly weigh in on the midterm results.

Former Republican House Speaker New Gingrich, in a post on X , suggested that the blowout midterm victory for Democrats ruined any chance for Vance to put an early lock on the party's nomination.

"The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open," Gingrich said. "If the administration had won a big victory, Vice President JD Vance would have had an enormous argument to be the inevitable nominee."

Trump told reporters said he thought the vice president's post-election assessment was "good." Asked about a potential Vance run in 2028, Trump said "we'll see what happens," and suggested that many others could also run. "Maybe he won't run," Trump said. "I don't know who's going to run. But I can tell you, as far as that war's concerned, I would have done nothing different."

Cruz: 'Understandably, people were pissed off'

Cruz framed Republicans' losses in historic terms after Democrats won the midterm popular vote by 13 percentage points ‒ the greatest margin in a midterm election since 1976 ‒ and he confronted a new reality in which he's "the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas."

"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami," Cruz said in a lengthy analysis on social media . "It was an ass kicking. It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation. What happened, and why? What are the consequences, and where on earth do we go from here?"

Cruz blamed Trump's tariffs for "making everything too expensive." He said the war in Iran has "dragged on too long" and "should have been brief, decisive, and over." He also said a "very real economic disconnect" hurt Republicans, pointing to expanding wealth for the super rich like Elon Musk and new data centers that are "turning billionaires into centimillionaires," while average Americans struggled with utility payments

"Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain," Cruz said, though he predicted that Democrats will "overshoot" and "overreach" by advancing policies that only drive up costs further.

Cruz, who is up for reelection next in 2030, vowed that Republicans will "rebuild as a true blue-collar party" and win back Texas.

'Fighting yesterday's battles,' DeSantis says

After their sweeping midterm losses in Texas ‒ where Republicans lost every statewide election, including for U.S. Senate ‒ the GOP can no longer bank on winning Texas and its 40 electoral votes in the next presidential election. Midterm wins for Sen.-elect James Talarico and other Texas Democrats instantly makes the Lonestar State a top battleground in 2028, giving Democrats a chance to severely hamper Republicans' electoral path to victory.

While Texas turned blue in the midterms, another Republican stronghold, Florida, remained in the Republican column ‒ a point that DeSantis was quick to emphasize as he sized up the midterms at a Nov. 4 press conference.

"So the question is, why did Florida hold up?" DeSantis said. "And I think the answer is that we've built up a record of achievement. We earned trust from a number of our voters, that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line."

Florida Republican Sen. Ashley Moody held off Democratic challenger Angie Nixon in Florida's Senate race, and Rep. Byron Donalds defeated Democrat David Jolly for governor to replace the term-limited DeSantis.

Nationally, however, DeSantis described a disastrous situation for Republicans, predicting that Democrats' strong majorities in the House and Senate could be so large that Republicans retaking either chamber in 2028 isn't even an option.

"We just have to be very clear-eyed. This is probably the worst-case scenario for a midterm election," DeSantis said.

DeSantis said he "knew Republicans were in trouble" when he saw Republican candidates were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads attacking transgender issues ‒ long a go-to cultural wedge issue for Republicans that they ran on successfully in 2024.

"Four years ago, we were in the peak 'woke era,'" DeSantis said. "It alienated a lot of people, rightfully so. It alienated me. So we were fighting back against that. Well, now the issues are different. And Republicans, it seemed like, in some of the ads I was seeing, they really were fighting yesterday's battles."

As for whether he will run in 2028, DeSantis said he will address that question after his term as governor ends in January.

"We'll talk about anything I'm doing on the other side of this," he said. "I've still got more work to do."

articles.title: Vance takes GOP hits as DeSantis, Cruz emerge as early GOP winners for 2028
articles.summary: The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP’s devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing c...
articles.body:
The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP's devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions.

The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance.

It's a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large.

"The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance's 2028 prospects," said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign.

"Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30's and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question," Madden added.

Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger.

"Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing," said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis.

"This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win," the operative added.

In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war.

"Vance's profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle," Madden predicted.

The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 "is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren't substantial changes."

If there aren't changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president.

DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind.

The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices.

In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of "gaslighting" voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety.

DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That's an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state.

Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion.

Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms.

On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP's terrible night.

He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs.

"Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high," he said.

GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday's results, their primary will be wide open.

"Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday," one former Trump campaign aide said. "It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance."

Other Republicans say Tuesday's results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field.

"Vance needs to announce first with the president's endorsement," said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. "If he doesn't do it in January, it'll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn't on board. And that's the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?"

One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there's "more space than less space" for other Republicans to enter the race.

"Let's face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night," the former aide said. "This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era."

The former aide added that Trump "is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that's 30 percent right off the bat."

But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances.

"Imagine, he's going to have to answer to Trump's whim or rant of the day every day," the former aide said. "And he's not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him.

"That's just not an enviable place," the former aide added.

Since the elections, Vance has been under scrutiny from both Republicans and Democrats. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who served under former President George W. Bush, took to social platform X to counter Vance's evaluation of the sweeping GOP losses.

"Please allow me to present a different perspective," Fleischer said. "The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire. If you start a war, you need to win it and finish it - otherwise don't start it."

Democrats also pounced on Vance's remarks.

"For you to reduce it to a simple political calculation while we still have 50,000 troops in the Middle East, is one of the most crass, cynical things I've seen," Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), wrote Wednesday on X. "You and President Trump got us into this war without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It's cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure with no end in sight."

On Thursday, as political pundits were saying it was the end of the Trump era, Republicans said Vance's political future remained murky at best.

"I think if you're Vance you gotta take the nomination and pray you get someone on the other side like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez," the first former Trump aide said, referring to the progressive representative from New York.

For now, Del Percio said, results aside, Vance "ultimately stands in the same place he did three weeks ago."

"He only exists at the whim of the president," she said. "And if Trump doesn't endorse, will Vance go without the president's endorsement? If he's forced to do that, he will break with Trump and it will get ugly."

articles.title: Gen Z men split from GOP in midterms, broke hard for Democrats
articles.summary: Tuesday was a big night for Democrats, and Generation Z was a big reason why. Young voters aged 18-29 broke hard for Democrats, including young men, who had...
articles.body:
Tuesday was a big night for Democrats, and Generation Z was a big reason why.

Young voters aged 18-29 broke hard for Democrats, including young men, who had been an important constituency for President Trump in 2024.

The voters were also a big part of the winning formula for the party in Texas, where some of the biggest wins of the night were recorded.

Trump won 56 percent of Gen Z men in 2024, per AP VoteCast data. But in 2026, Democrats pulled them across the aisle.

Fifty-nine percent of white men aged 18-29 voted Democratic on Tuesday, according to an analysis from Tufts University's Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE).

"The number one force driving young men to vote for Trump and Republicans in 2024 were promises about an improved economy. Most Americans, including Gen Z men, feel that the economy is now worse," said Tyler Daniel, an assistant professor of political science at Roanoke University.

This doesn't necessarily mean that young men have had a significant change in politics. It seems more like negative partisanship, or the concept of voting against, rather than for, a candidate or party.

Daniel, however, had expected them to sit out of the midterms. "This is an abnormal reaction from this age cohort when they feel disenfranchised by the political system," he said.

Adam Pennings, executive director of Run Gen Z, an organization that recruits and mentors young conservative candidates, said the young voters who came to Trump in 2024 are the same ones who left in 2026.

"Gen Z is the cost of living generation, and they voted like it," Pennings added. "A lot of Republicans didn't realize how pessimistic young people were, specifically."

The data shows it — the Harvard Youth Poll reported that only 9 percent of young adults said the country was headed in the right direction. For the first time in its history, the poll said that more respondents expected to be financially worse off than their parents, not better, at 27 percent and 25 percent, respectively.

While Democrats hammered messages on affordability, Republicans spoke of the culture war, which led young men to vote for the candidates who campaigned on lowering prices.

"Under the first Trump administration, the economy was better. Younger voters, especially younger men, may have been more likely to give Republicans a chance again in 2024," said Melissa Deckman, CEO of the Public Religion Research Institute. While cultural issues were still relevant in the previous election, Gen Z men mostly voted by looking at their wallets.

"There's a sense that the American dream is out of reach," Deckman added.

Now, Democrats face pressure to deliver on their campaign promises.

"This is not a generation of folks who will acquiesce to transactional interactions. There's a desire for candidates to show up with authenticity," said Leela Strong, a director at CIRCLE.

Looking toward 2028, Daniel expects that the GOP will prepare to lead the America First movement that is currently splintering within the party. He pointed to podcasters Tucker Carlson and Nick Fuentes, both of whom are trying to capitalize on points that the MAGA movement originally made with Gen Z men.

"We will have to see whether or not MAGA can exist without Trump guiding politics," Daniel said. "The Republican Party is going through a broader identity crisis, one that will only worsen once Trump leaves power in 2029, and it is too early to see where Gen Z men will fall into the mix."

Gen Z made up 12 percent the midterm vote

Data from The New York Times found that 70 percent of voters aged 18-29 cast their ballots for Democrats, a 33-point shift from 2024.

The red-blue divide was striking in some reliably Republican states like Texas and Alabama, where 70 percent and 63 percent, respectively, backed Democratic candidates.

Only in South Dakota and West Virginia did a majority of Gen Z voters support the Republican candidate. And the margins were slim, with the GOP reaching just a 2-point and 3-point lead in South Dakota and West Virginia, respectively.

President Trump led former Vice President Kamala Harris by 30 points is South Dakota and 42 points in West Virginia among voters aged 18-29, according to exit polls.

Those figures were similar to the vote in the 2020 presidential election , where Trump led former President Biden by 18 points in South Dakota and 32 points in West Virginia.

Exit polling from The Associated Press found that across all generations, the economy remained voters' top priority. But Gen Zers were most likely to say they cast their vote as a rejection of Trump, in line with earlier reporting that younger Americans were more likely to say they regretted voting for the current president.

Kimberly McGuire, the executive director at URGE, a reproductive justice organization that partnered with HIT Strategies for a national survey of young voters , said the cost of living drove Tuesday's results and that neither party should take Gen Z for granted.

"I think there is so much to learn from this election about how Gen Z has really found their feet politically," McGuire told The Hill. "Some of the things that are rising to the top are the way in which Gen Z voters should not be taken for granted and should be treated in many ways as a swing constituency."

Going into Tuesday's midterm elections, all eyes were on Texas.

State Rep. James Talarico (D) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) were locked in a highly contested battle for Sen. John Cornyn's (R-Texas) Senate seat, while State Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) looked to unseat Gov. Greg Abbott (R).

Both races ultimately swung in the Democrats' favor in historic wins for the party, and Democrats believe young voters played a huge role.

An exit poll from The New York Times found that 74 percent of people aged 18-29 voted for Talarico in this year's Texas Senate race — a 49 point boost for Democrats compared to the 2024 election.

Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party, noted that Gen Z "was a huge part of our coalition," but there was no one group of Texans that drove Talarico's and Hinojosa's wins.

"What we did see consistently were people with low propensity, people who didn't vote very often, maybe hadn't voted before, showing up in much larger numbers than you would expect for a midterm," Scudder said.

Texas has historically ranked 49th in the country for voter turnout, making it a big deal that younger generations flocked to the polls.

Talarico's and Hinojosa's campaign strategies to increase voter turnout targeted Gen Z, using tech-savvy, snappier techniques that Scudder believes worked in their favor.

"They weren't necessarily just leaning on legacy media to get their messaging. You saw them running strong social media plans across different platforms, they had very functional TikToks, very functional Instagrams," Scudder said. "It allowed them to reach people, get their message across and express the urgency — meeting people where they are."

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We're working to understand the ins and outs of our generation's politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Republicans eye 2028 presidential bids after midterm rebuke
articles.summary: Administration figures including the vice president and secretary of state all face headwinds over their links to US President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Republican leaders took early steps signaling potential 2028 presidential bids, using disastrous midterm elections to distance themselves from the Trump administration. Florida's governor, who unsuccessfully sought the GOP nomination in 2024, has been among the loudest critics of Republican leadership in recent days and did not rule out running in the next presidential race while on CNN.

Administration figures including the vice president — whose post blaming midterms losses on the Iran war was seen as a sign of his Oval Office ambitions — secretary of state, and defense secretary all face headwinds over their links to US President Donald Trump. Beyond intra-party fights, however, one person close to the White House told Semafor, " The actual question is: Can any Republican win? "

articles.title: ABC's 'The View' hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day, MRC study finds
articles.summary: ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day this season, according to a Media Research Center study of its guest list.
articles.body:
ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest and 21 liberal guests in the weeks leading up to Election Day, according to a new study by the conservative media watchdog Media Research Center (MRC).

The study found that from Sept. 8, the start of Season 30, through Nov. 3, "The View" invited 21 liberal guests who were either critical of President Donald Trump or the Republican Party, with Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, being the lone conservative guest.

Four of the guests classified as liberal were politicians: Gov. Andy Beshear, D-Ky.; Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz.; Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who appeared on the show the day before Election Day alongside liberal podcast host Kara Swisher.

Although a retiring Republican senator, Tillis was included in the liberal guest count due to being invited on to discuss his anti-Trump book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents."

Tillis has been vocal in calling for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's firing and has publicly broken with the president over the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill. In his book, Tillis wrote that he hoped Republicans would learn from midterm losses, which he predicted when the book was released in early October.

"What I hope is that members of my party take the loss and learn something," he wrote, according to The New York Times, "specifically that putting party affiliation — or loyalty to one man — before your own conscience never turns out well in the end."

The show hosted several liberal celebrities as well, including Maisie Williams, Ethan Hawke, Chelsea Handler, Michael Douglas, Billy Crystal, Patricia "Ms. Pat" Williams-Lee, D.L. Hughley, Chandra Wilson, Busy Philipps, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Eisa Davis, Jamie Lee Curtis and Sophia Bush.

Neil deGrasse Tyson and Stephen A. Smith were among the other guests included in the study. Smith appeared on the show to discuss his recent White House meeting with Trump, a decision that drew criticism from the co-hosts. He defended his decision to attend. The ESPN host also criticized the president during the appearance.

According to the study's methodology, guests had to express liberal or conservative views during their appearances on the talk show to be counted in either category.

"If a celebrity did not discuss politics, they were not included in the count of political leanings even if they had a history of being outspoken in the past," the MRC said.

The show hosted 56 guests in total between Sept. 8 and Nov. 3, according to the study.

The daytime talk show drew scrutiny in 2025 after hosting 128 liberal guests over the course of the year and just two conservatives. In 2026, the show hosted Vice President JD Vance and Alina Habba, a former legal spokesperson for Trump. The show also had several Republican fill-in co-hosts while Alyssa Farah Griffin was on maternity leave. The fill-ins included Elisabeth Hasselbeck and Savannah Chrisley, among others.

In January 2026, the co-hosts interviewed former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Republican who became a fierce Trump critic.

"The View" did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

MRC President David Bozell said in a statement, "ABC has learned nothing from the FCC's continued scrutiny. 'The View' continues to insult the intelligence of the American public by passing off pure Democratic propaganda as a 'bona fide news program.'"

"With 21 anti-Republican voices and a single conservative in the two months before the midterms, ABC's political agenda could hardly be more obvious," he continued. "And ABC is hardly alone. The entire elitist media landscape deserves serious scrutiny. The Federal Communications Commission must hold ABC accountable for its abuse of the public airwaves for partisan political purposes."

The program has faced a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) investigation over the past year. ABC has responded by defending "The View" as a "bona fide news" program.

The investigation is related to the agency's crackdown on equal-time requirements for political candidates. A source at the FCC told Fox News Digital in February that the show's interview with James Talarico triggered the probe.

"'The View' has been broadcasting under a bona fide news exemption granted to it more than twenty years ago ... The Commission has taken no action over the last two decades to modify or overturn the Declaratory Ruling and there is no basis for doing so now," ABC said in a petition in May in response to the FCC's probe.

The co-hosts interviewed Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico on Wednesday after he won his election in Texas and interviewed Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday after his election victory.

Republican Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who won her re-election campaign, is going to appear on the program next week.

articles.title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
articles.summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected...
articles.body:
The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections , as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades .

The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.

Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:

Democrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.

Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system , which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.

Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains a toss-up . State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities to flip a House seat, after moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Golden's decision not to run for reelection set the stage for a contest between former GOP Gov. Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap. Even though Dunlap conceded , officials in Maine say the race will proceed to a ranked-choice tabulation because LePage was just shy of the 50% mark. The tabulation will start Nov. 9.

Florida's 9th District: This was one of four districts that Florida Republicans tilted to the right in a pre-midterm redistricting campaign — and the only one that hasn't yet been projected as a Democratic win. Democratic Rep. Darren Soto is trying to stave off a challenge from Republican Dan Green.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate is close to a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it could go to a runoff next month.

Several races held by Republicans still don't have projections — including in districts that Democrats are hoping to flip.

Colorado's 3rd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd is trying to hold on to this largely rural district, and faces a challenge from Democrat Dwayne Romero.

Colorado's 4th District: Firebrand Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert is running against Democrat Eileen Laubacher. Boebert switched to the district two years ago, after narrowly winning reelection in a more competitive district in 2022.

Florida's 7th District: Republican Ryan Elijah is running against Democrat Bale Dalton, after Elijah defeated the scandal-plagued GOP Rep. Cory Mills in a primary. The district has historically leaned red.

Florida's 26th District: GOP Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Nicole Locklin in South Florida.

Florida's 27th District: It's a battle between two former Miami-area news anchors — GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar and Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. Salazar made waves earlier this year when she warned President Trump's immigration policies could alienate Latino voters.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is locked in a tight battle against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount .

Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.

North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans .

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.

North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.

North Carolina's 8th District: GOP Rep. Mark Harris is facing Democrat Colby Watson.

North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.

New York's 21st District: Republican Anthony Constantino is running against Democrat Blake Gendebien in a red-leaning Upstate district left open by GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik's decision not to seek reelection .

South Carolina's 1st District: This coastal district — held by outgoing GOP Rep. Nancy Mace — is hosting a competitive contest between Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a member of the Charleston County Council, and Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral who was among those fired during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's tenure.

South Carolina's 2nd District: Longtime Republican Rep. Joe Wilson is running against Democrat Zyon Khalifa.

Arizona's 2nd District: In a rematch of 2024, Republican Rep. Eli Crane is running against Democrat Jonathan Nez.

Arizona's 5th District: Republican Mark Lamb is running against Democrat Elizabeth Lee in a district left open by GOP Rep. Andy Biggs' decision to run for governor.

Arizona's 8th District: Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh is running against Democrat Bernadette Greene-Placentia .

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed .

California's 4th District: In the Napa Valley area, longtime Rep. Mike Thompson is running against businessman and fellow Democrat Eric Jones .

California's 7th District: This seat was changed significantly by redistricting. Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui is running against another Democrat, Mai Vang.

California's 11th District: Democrats Scott Wiener and Connie Chan are battling for the San Francisco district long held by retiring Rep. Nancy Pelosi.

California's 14th District: Democrats Melissa Hernandez and Rep. Aisha Wahab are running in a district previously held by Rep. Eric Swalwell , who resigned amid sexual misconduct allegations — which he denied.

California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

California's 40th District: After California's redistricting campaign last year scrambled the House districts in Southern California, incumbent Republican Reps. Ken Calvert and Young Kim are running against each other to represent parts of Orange County and the Inland Empire.

Washington's 4th District: Republican Amanda McKinney and Democrat John Duresky are running for the district held by retiring Rep. Dan Newhouse, one of the only remaining Republicans who voted to impeach Mr. Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot.

Washington's 5th District: In Eastern Washington, GOP Rep. Michael Baumgartner is running against Democrat Carmela Conroy.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate this week.

Utah's 4th District: GOP Rep. Mike Kennedy is running for reelection against Democrat Jonny Larsen.

articles.title: Meet the teens who won their midterm election races
articles.summary: Daniel Darris-O'Connor and Sebastian Matta were in elementary school when President Donald Trump was first elected.
articles.body:
They were in elementary school when President Donald Trump was first elected. And now they're set to hold elected office themselves.

Two 19-year-olds won their respective midterm elections on Nov. 3 for seats at the local level: state representative and county clerk.

Both Democrats, they prevailed over veteran politicians in an election cycle now defined by a resounding repudiation of Trump and the GOP.

Daniel Darris-O'Connor, 19, of Billerica, Massachusetts, was elected state representative for the 22nd Middlesex district, unseating a longtime Republican incumbent.

In Arizona, 19-year-old Sebastian Matta won his race for Maricopa County Clerk of the Superior Court.

"I'm a full-time college student who just, you know, happens to be doing a side gig running for office," Matta said in a Nov. 5 interview on "Jimmy Kimmel Live."

Meet the newly-elected officials and other young candidates making history.

Byron Donalds celebrates historic victory as Florida’s first Black governor

19-year-old Darris-O'Connor says he was mistaken for an intern

Darris-O'Connor, who unseated 16-year Republican incumbent Marc Lombardo, will be sworn in as state representative one day after his 20th birthday in January.

He told CBS News Boston that his interest in politics began when he was in seventh grade during the COVID-19 pandemic. After joining several local boards and committees, he was elected to the Billerica Select Board in 2025 as a high school senior.

Although his age is making headlines, Darris-O'Connor has said in interviews with several local media outlets that his campaign wasn't focused on that. Still, it didn't come without some confusion on the campaign trail.

"Sometimes people thought I was the candidate's son. Some people thought that I was an intern with the campaign, but some of those lighthearted initial interactions led into substantive discussions about the campaign and the issues at stake," he told CBS News Boston.

A student at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Darris-O'Connor told 7 News WHDH that he intends to serve his district full time after completing his international relations degree.

Sebastian Matta says he's 'not just an ordinary 19-year-old'

Sebastian Matta lives with his parents and took his opponents' concession call over a Chipotle bowl. But he says he's "not just an ordinary 19-year-old."

"It takes a certain caliber of 19-year-old to collect 4,063 signatures, to get on the ballot, to raise $20,000 from over nine different states, to go to all 25 or so legislative districts in Maricopa County and drive almost 30,000 miles doing that," he told The Arizona Republic, part of the USA TODAY Network.

Matta told The Republic that he decided to run for office after turning 18 in 2025. The Maricopa County Clerk role piqued his interest because he used to travel to the office with his father, an investigator for a law firm, to submit documents for personal injury cases.

"I saw that nobody on the Democratic side had submitted themselves to this office in nearly a decade," he said. "And I figured, 'You know, why not?'"

The teen ran against Republican Jeff Dial, a former state senator, for the seat that has not been held by Democrats for several decades.

Although Matta, a student at Arizona State University, told the Republic he thought his bid would be a "destined loss," he said he was "overwhelmed with happiness" when he won.

"I mean, this whole running for office thing has been a very much a day-by-day thing. And my future aspirations are a problem for Sebastian in four years who can drink," Matta told Kimmel.

O'Connor and Matta aren't the only members of Gen Z who have stepped up for political office, or made history doing it.

Dawson Holle, a Republican North Dakota state representative, became the state's youngest elected lawmaker at age 18 in 2022. Now 22, he was reelected to another term on Nov. 3.

In New Hampshire, State Rep. Valerie McDonnell was also elected in 2022 at age 18. A Republican, she is the youngest person in state history to be elected to the office. While she is up for another term, McDonnell's race has yet to be called ; with 99% of the vote in as of late Nov. 4, she is the seventh-top vote-getter in a race with nine winners, according to the Associated Press.

And in the national political landscape, this election cycle also produced a new youngest member of Congress. The title goes to Michael Alfonso , the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy , who won in Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District.

How old do you have to be to run for office?

Minimum age of candidacy depends on the office.

For U.S. Senate , officeholders must be at least 30 years old, while U.S. representatives have to be at least 25.

On the state-level, the age requirements vary. For the Massachusetts House and Maricopa County court clerk roles, candidates must be at least 18 years old.

Melina Khan is a national trending reporter for USA TODAY. Keep up with her on Instagram @bymelinakhan and TikTok @melina.khan2 .

articles.title: The fight is growing over ballot counting in Mississippi’s tight Senate race
articles.summary: National party operatives, lawyers, grassroots activists and content creators are descending on Mississippi to observe the vetting of thousands of provisiona...
articles.body:
National party operatives, lawyers, grassroots activists and content creators are descending on Mississippi to observe the vetting of thousands of provisional ballots in the coming days and to gear up for possible legal challenges over the final results.

Mississippi, a state not used to the national spotlight for close elections, now sits at the forefront of a fight that will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the US Senate next year.

Democrat Scott Colom has a razor-thin lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, in a state that hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 40 years and no Black person to the Senate since Reconstruction.

Both Colom and Hyde-Smith have assembled extensive teams ready to observe and potentially challenge ballot-counting procedures ahead of Mississippi's December 3 deadline for certifying the results.

"We were prepared for this for months," Colom told reporters Wednesday. "We have an army of lawyers. We have local lawyers. We have everybody involved to make sure the process is followed according to the law."

At a press conference Thursday, the state GOP touted the 50-plus volunteer attorneys and observers it had sent across the state, and Mississippi Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst said many more are prepared to jump in to help.

"Our attorneys and observers will continue to be in different parts of Mississippi – watching as election commissioners review and process these outstanding ballots, ensuring that our elections are followed and that only ballots which have been legally cast are counted," he said.

The nonpartisan NAACP also is engaged in post-election work.

NAACP members and volunteers are being deployed to all of the state's 82 counties to monitor how election officials vet outstanding provisional ballots – known as "affidavit" ballots in Mississippi – cast because the voters lacked photo ID or were not showing up in their precincts' poll books.

In cases in which a voter failed to provide identification, the NAACP's volunteers will scramble to contact voters and encourage them to head to the county courthouse with the proper documentation.

Tuesday is the deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues on provisional ballots and also for counties to receive absentee ballots postmarked on or before Election Day. Counties must certify their results by November 13.

"Our interest is no individual, particularly African Americans, disenfranchised in this process because of lack of ID," NAACP President Derrick Johnson told CNN.

One voter in Hinds County, home to Jackson, told CNN about how she cast a ballot for Colom this week. Dajia Williams, 23, said she updated her driver's license and voter registration in May after moving to Hinds from a nearby county.

She said she checked the online registration on the Sunday before the election to make sure she was there and grew concerned when she couldn't spot her name. Williams, who voted in the primary and presidential elections in 2024, figured the change hadn't posted yet.

But on Election Day, poll workers couldn't find her either. The election official provided her with a provisional ballot and told her to go to the circuit court and show her ID again, even though she'd brought it to the polls.

"I don't feel like people should have to feel like they're jumping through hoops to to go vote, especially in Mississippi," she told CNN, adding that "a lot of people don't even know what an affidavit or a provisional ballot is."

It's not clear how many provisional ballots remain to be counted. Officials in Colom's campaign pegged the number at 15,000 earlier this week. Republicans estimated that as many as 20,000 absentee ballots and provisional ballots were outstanding as of Thursday afternoon.

Secretary of State Michael Watson has said the total number is unknown.

Colom told CNN that he was optimistic his lead – at about 1,800 votes late Thursday – would continue to grow as more ballots were counted.

"You look at the ballots that are left, you know, it's going in our favor," he said.

Intense scrutiny of ballots and counties

The proceedings during which county election committees announce whether to accept or reject a provisional ballot are open to the public, but the levels of transparency vary county to county, advocates say.

Dueling letters sent to local election officials Thursday from the Democratic and Republican attorneys showcased the intense scrutiny the state will be under.

A letter from the law firm representing the Hyde-Smith campaign requested that local officials segregate affidavit ballots from the rest of the count, and that they preserve other election-related records.

Colom's lawyers shot back Thursday night with a letter of their own calling the request "unlawful," and warning against taking any step that would allow "particular ballot to be traced to a particular voter," in violation of ballot secrecy laws.

In the state's largest county that is home to Jackson, county commissioners are sorting through hundreds of affidavit ballots in a way that is open for the public to observe. One commissioner has over 600 affidavits to manage, and on Thursday was trying to make a dent in the 233 affidavit ballots from students at Jackson State University. Hinds County Election Commissioner Felicia McClinton said she had to reject a number of them because the young voters were not registered in the right precinct.

In one instance, McClinton tried searching for a college student's birthday, name, and social security number but could not locate her in the system.

"This will be rejected," McClinton told CNN, as representatives from the Colom campaign looked on and took notes.

The tight race may have been a shock to some across the country, but Democrats say they began preparing early for the possibility that the results could come down to a small number of votes, requiring close attention to Mississippi's election procedures.

The Elias Law Group – a voting rights law firm aligned with Democrats – ramped up its attention Mississippi's election protocols in early 2026, using a team of researchers set up within the firm called the Election Protection Intelligence Collaborative. The work included monitoring in-state media, watching meetings of local election commissions, and developing a granular level of knowledge about how elections are run in the state.

Lawyers for the firm, which is representing the Colom campaign, began arriving in Mississippi on Wednesday.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also recently deployed lawyers and resources for the state, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

Fair Fight PAC, a voting rights focused political organization founded by Stacey Abrams, is playing a central role, working with the Colom campaign and the DSCC.

Mississippi Votes, a nonpartisan civic organization, has set up a voter information hotline and virtual phone banking to help anyone who has questions about the ballot curing process as volunteers from across the country arrive to help the effort.

Lily Moens, the policy and research director at Mississippi Votes, told CNN that her team is hearing that the majority of ballots that are being rejected are because voters tried to vote at the incorrect precincts.

"It's disheartening to see folks' ballots being rejected because they were just at the wrong location," Moens said.

In one sign of the national focus on Mississippi, Jess Craven, a progressive activist and content creator, flew to Jackson this week from her home in Los Angeles at the invitation of the NAACP. She said she was there to "make sure that every vote is counted."

"It's not just about picking up another seat," Craven said. "It's about a seismic event in the South that's long overdue."

In an interview with CNN on Thursday, Colom said it took him months to get his party and the nation to pay attention to his Senate race in Mississippi.

Without specifying how many lawyers and representatives he has, Colom said he has "enough" resources, including a late influx of cash from an aggressive fundraising push.

"I'm confident about where we are," he said. "I'm glad people are doing what it takes to get us over the finish line."

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Fair Fight PAC is working with the Colom campaign and the DSCC.

Grayer reported from Jackson, Mississippi. CNN's Aleena Fayaz and Allison Gordon contributed to this report.
